newsitem.title: KENYA: Rwanda genocide tribunal delays key case.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda genocide tribunal delays key case.

text.p: The international tribunal for Rwanda has put off the key genocide trial of a Rwandan leader accused of firing a starting pistol to signal mass slaughter in 1994, officials said on Thursday.

Tribunal information chief Beatrice Lacoste said by telephone from Arusha, Tanzania, the case of Clement Kayishema was postponed on Wednesday until February 20 and he was ordered tried with fellow accused, Obed Ruzindana.

It was the latest of a long series of setbacks for the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in its attempt to bring to justice leaders of the 1994 genocide by Hutus of up to one million Tutsis and Hutu moderates.

Prosecutors say Kayishema, prefect of Kibuye on the border with now war-torn east Zaire, herded his region's Tutsis into Catholic churches and a town stadium, fired the starting pistol and joined his militiamen in the ensuing orgy of killing.
"The attackers used guns, grenades, pangas, machetes, spears, cudgels and their weapons to kill the people in the stadium," his May 31 indictment read.
In the genocide an estimated 800,000 of the 930,000 Tutsis in Rwanda were killed.
Kayishema has pleaded not guilty to all 25 counts of genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the Geneva convention. He is accused of being responsible for thousands of deaths.
The trial was scheduled to begin in earnest on Thursday but Presiding Judge Laity Kama postponed it on Wednesday, a day after a preliminary hearing that aired many of the tribunal's woes.
Prosecutors told Kama fresh conflict in Zaire just across the border from Kibuye had brought fresh chaos to the area where his key witnesses, whose protection was already difficult, are still living.
For the Arusha-based tribunal trying to show the world that perpetrators of genocide will not escape, a Tutsi rebel offensive through eastern Zaire was an added blow.
Defence lawyer Andre Ferran complained at the hearing that he had not got key documents on time and said he was underpaid, his work underfunded and that he had been given no assistant.
After failing to win a longer delay until March, arguing he had been given insufficient time to prepare his case, he told prosecutors he may quit and return to France, Lacoste said.
On October 31 the tribunal put off until January another major trial, that of Jean Paul Akayesu, another former government official accused of genocide.
Rwanda's Tutsi-led government which took power after the genocide has accused the tribunal of descending into farce.
The tribunal has indicted 21 people, 12 of whom are in custody. Other suspects are among Rwandan Hutu refugees in Zaire.
More than 80,000 other suspects are in Rwandan jails where, unlike at the tribunal, they face the death penalty.
A U.N. official visited Arusha last month as part of a U.N. investigation amid charges that the slow-moving judicial process to bring to justice genocide leaders has been paralysed by its own staff.
